cards.text: The Song of Songs is a love poem between a young woman and the man she calls her beloved (Song of Solomon 2:16). Now voices call out to her, the Shulammite: “Come back, come back,” and then they say it AGAIN. Four “come backs,” friend, and I've had alarm clocks with less commitment than that.

cards.question: The voices want the Shulammite to come back so they can gaze upon her.

answers.text: True
False

cards.text: Then comes a question: “Why do you look at the Shulammite, as on the dance of Mahanaim?” Earlier in the Song, a description of her started up top with her eyes (Song of Solomon 4:1), but this time the description takes the scenic route.

cards.question: This time, the description of the Shulammite starts at her head and works its way down to her feet.

answers.text: True
False

cards.text: Up it climbs, starting with “How beautiful are your sandaled feet, O daughter of the prince!” Then come her thighs like jewels, her navel and her waist, and her breasts, “like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.”

Then her neck is “like a tower made of ivory,” her eyes like the pools of Heshbon, and her nose like the tower of Lebanon. Meanwhile, the nicest thing anybody ever said to ME was my oven timer going BEEP, and even that was just to tell me I burned the batch.

cards.question: At the top, the Shulammite's head crowns her like Mount Carmel and her hair is like purple threads. Then comes the line “the king is captured in your tresses.” What is that picture saying?

answers.text: The king is drawn in by her beauty
The king has been locked in a prison
The king is hiding from his enemies

cards.text: Then the speaker steps back and takes it all in: “How fair and pleasant you are, O love, with your delights!” And then: “Your stature is like a palm tree; your breasts are clusters of fruit.”

cards.question: After saying the Shulammite's stature is like a palm tree and her breasts are clusters of fruit, the speaker says, “I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit.” What is that picture showing?

answers.text: The speaker longs to be close to her
The speaker wants to gather a harvest
The speaker plans to guard her from others

cards.text: Next come wishes: that her breasts be like clusters of the vine, her breath like apples, and her mouth like the finest wine. Then the line turns: “May it flow smoothly to my beloved, gliding gently over lips and teeth.”

cards.question: Then the Shulammite speaks up with one short line about who she belongs to. What does she say?

answers.text: She belongs to her beloved and he desires her
She belongs to her brothers and must work for them
She belongs to her people and must stay home

cards.question: Right after that, the Shulammite invites her beloved to the countryside to spend the night among the wildflowers.

answers.text: True
False

cards.text: And after that, she wants them off to the vineyards, and not just any time, but EARLY. Friend, some of us need a whole batch of cookies before we can even SAY the word “early.”

cards.question: Early in the vineyards, what does the Shulammite want to see?

answers.text: If the vine has budded and the blossom opened
If the grapes are ripe and ready to pick
If the vines have been pruned and tied up

cards.text: And there, she says, she'll give him her love. Even the mandrakes are sending out their fragrance.

cards.question: At their door, the Shulammite says, is every delicacy, new as well as old, that she has treasured up for her ___.

answers.text: beloved
sisters
guests

cards.text: Then she makes a wish: that her beloved were like a brother to her. Stay with me, friend, because she tells us exactly WHY.

cards.question: Why does the Shulammite wish her beloved were like a brother to her?

answers.text: So she could kiss him outdoors and not be despised
So they could share the family vineyard together
So they could inherit their father's land together

cards.question: The Shulammite says she would lead her beloved to the house of her ___, who taught her, and give him spiced wine to drink.

answers.text: mother
master
king

cards.text: Then comes a line that also shows up earlier in the Song (Song of Solomon 2:6): “His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me.” And she closes with a charge she's given twice before (Song of Solomon 2:7; 3:5), and friend, when something gets said THREE times, that's not a suggestion: “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.”
